items.title: Jim Cramer says Wall Street is fleeing the AI trade and buying these stocks instead
items.summary:
"The stocks just anticipate the ending," he added.

Take Western Digital, the stock hit an all-time closing high of $746 per share on June 18 — at the time, up 333% for the year. Less than six weeks later, the stock is down nearly 40% from its record.

Cramer stressed, however, that investors are not abandoning the market altogether. Instead, they are redeploying capital into companies whose growth depends less on continued AI infrastructure spending. [...] Prime examples are Micron, Western Digital, Seagate, and Sandisk, whose shares soared as shortages of memory used in AI servers gave the companies unprecedented pricing power. After peaking in June, those stocks have tumbled as investors bet those shortages — and the extraordinary profits they created — won't last forever.

"I have been through many boom-bust cycles with these companies," Cramer said. "You have to sell the parabolic moves that these shortages trigger because they always end." [...] CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that Wall Street is taking profits in this year's biggest AI infrastructure winners and rotating into stocks of companies with growth drivers away from the data center.

"You can call it a broadening," the "Mad Money" host said. "Or you can call it fleeing."

Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence data center buildout dominated the market for much of the first half of the year, but many of them have pulled back sharply in recent weeks.

items.title: OPENAI IS SO WORRIED THEY HAVE PAUSED TRAINING
items.summary:
OPENAI IS SO WORRIED THEY HAVE PAUSED TRAINING

“This is the first security incident that I have felt very viscerally. I've been a little surprised that more people don't feel it so viscerally.

We paused training. We have to figure out how to secure our sandboxing in a world of multiple zero days being chained together.

We may have to pace the rate of AI development to give ourselves enough time for society to harden around these new capability levels."

items.title: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:

"by March of 2028, we will have a full end to end, very talented researcher figuring out completely new architectures."

Not an assistant. Not autocomplete for scientists. A system that does the research that produces the next system.

In 1965 the statistician I. J. Good wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention man need ever make. For sixty years that sentence lived in philosophy papers. Altman just put it on a roadmap with a quarter attached.

He also says: "with an affordable amount of spend on tokens, you can do what a 100-person, incredibly great engineering team would do as a startup."

Sixty years of arguing about whether the last invention is possible. Nobody expected the answer to arrive as a delivery date.

items.title: Gilbert Strang, a quiet MIT professor, picked up a piece of chalk and explained the one skill standing between you and e
items.summary:
Gilbert Strang, a quiet MIT professor, picked up a piece of chalk and explained the one skill standing between you and every account you have ever blown.

MIT put the entire course online. it has been free for over twenty years. almost nobody finishes it.

His point: the market never pays in certainties. it pays in probabilities, and a human gut can barely hold one straight. the math that holds ten thousand at once, weighs them, and collapses them into a single call is linear algebra. it is the branch Citadel and OpenAI both pay $400K to hire for.

he is not a trading guru. his 18.06 lectures are the most watched math class on the planet.

Skip to where he turns a wall of numbers into one vector. a single object carrying a thousand odds at once, in notation a beginner can follow.

No slides. no jargon. one piece of chalk.

a quant I know rewatches lecture one every year before he sizes a single position.

You do not have a strategy problem. you have a math problem. the fix has been free for two decades, and you are still guessing.

items.title: 「AIでコードを書くのをやめて、第二の脳を作れ」と海外で話題になってるので共有。
items.summary:
「AIでコードを書くのをやめて、第二の脳を作れ」と海外で話題になってるので共有。
OpenAIの共同創業者Karpathyが出した"第二の脳"のやり方はこう↓

・Obsidian（無料のメモアプリ）を入れて、vaultを作る

・そのvaultをClaude Codeで開いて、Karpathyの設計メモ（wikiのアイデアを書いた1枚）を渡して「これ作って」と言う

・AIが箱を3つ用意する（raw＝素材用／wiki＝AIが整えたページ用／CLAUDE. md＝動かすルール1枚）

・rawに素材（記事・PDF・文字起こし）を放り込んで「取り込んで」と言う

・あとは全部を横断して、いつでも聞ける

セットアップは5分。これで、白紙のチャットから毎回始めなくてよくなる。

なんでまだみんなこれを使ってないのか、本気で分からない。

items.title: SAM ALTMAN CALLED OPENAI A "COMPANY" TO ELON MUSK'S FACE IN 2015.
items.summary:
SAM ALTMAN CALLED OPENAI A "COMPANY" TO ELON MUSK'S FACE IN 2015.

Elon stopped him cold.

"OpenAI is structured as a 501(c)3 nonprofit."

Not a company. A nonprofit. Built specifically so no one would ever profit from it.

Sam nodded.

Then spent the next 10 years running it.

Then converted it into a for-profit company valued at $300 billion.

With shareholders.

With investors expecting returns.

The correction Elon gave him in that interview was not a small vocabulary note.

It was the entire point of OpenAI's existence.

The nonprofit structure was not a legal technicality.

It was the promise.

The thing that made it different from every other AI lab racing to make money.

Sam knew that in 2015.

He was corrected on it by the co-founder in real time.

And then he changed the structure anyway.

The interview exists.

The correction is on tape.

The conversion happened.

@elonmusk
 is in court arguing this exact point right now.

The evidence is the 2015 interview.

Screenshot this.

Follow @cyrilXBT for every OpenAI development the mainstream refuses to connect the dots on.

"The stocks just anticipate the ending," he added.

Take Western Digital, the stock hit an all-time closing high of $746 per share on June 18 — at the time, up 333% for the year. Less than six weeks later, the stock is down nearly 40% from its record.

Cramer stressed, however, that investors are not abandoning the market altogether. Instead, they are redeploying capital into companies whose growth depends less on continued AI infrastructure spending. [...] Prime examples are Micron, Western Digital, Seagate, and Sandisk, whose shares soared as shortages of memory used in AI servers gave the companies unprecedented pricing power. After peaking in June, those stocks have tumbled as investors bet those shortages — and the extraordinary profits they created — won't last forever.

"I have been through many boom-bust cycles with these companies," Cramer said. "You have to sell the parabolic moves that these shortages trigger because they always end." [...] CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that Wall Street is taking profits in this year's biggest AI infrastructure winners and rotating into stocks of companies with growth drivers away from the data center.

"You can call it a broadening," the "Mad Money" host said. "Or you can call it fleeing."

Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence data center buildout dominated the market for much of the first half of the year, but many of them have pulled back sharply in recent weeks.

On July 16, Hugging Face said it had been hit by an unusually automated cyberattack. items.title: OpenAI vs Hugging Face: The Irony Is Off The Charts
items.summary:
OpenAI vs Hugging Face: The Irony Is Off The Charts

OpenAI's evaluation models allegedly escaped their sandbox, targeted Hugging Face's infrastructure, and triggered one of the most talked-about AI security stories of the year. But the biggest irony came after the attack.  When Hugging Face began investigating the incident, commercial frontier models reportedly refused to analyze the forensic data because of their safety guardrails. Instead, the team turned to an open-weight model running locally to complete the investigation.  In this episode, we break down what was reported, why many researchers are questioning parts of the narrative, and what this reveals about the current state of AI safety, hosted APIs, and open-weight models. We also explore why the real security conversation may have less to do with the language model itself and more to do with the systems, tools, and infrastructure built around it.  If your business is evaluating AI strategy, cybersecurity, or local AI infrastructure, this is a discussion you won't want to miss.
